title: Linux md RAID Degraded Array Detection
exclusions: This use case covers active Linux Multiple Devices (md) arrays exposed under `/sys/block/md*/md` and alerts only when the kernel's `degraded` attribute is greater than zero. It does not cover hardware-controller RAID, firmware RAID that is not presented through md, ZFS or Btrfs redundancy, RAID0 or linear devices with no redundant member semantics, stopped or disappeared arrays that no longer have a sysfs directory, spare-count policy, latent sector errors, parity mismatch counts, filesystem health, backup recoverability, or data-integrity assurance. The primary SPL contains no maintenance lookup or other suppression.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_md_raid_degraded_array_10m` saved-search definition, scheduler and alert history, and result exports containing `observed_at`, `host`, `md_device`, `raid_level`, `raid_disks`, `degraded_devices`, `array_state`, `sync_action`, `sync_completed`, `rebuild_percent`, and `faulty_components`. Preserve the corresponding raw `linux:md_raid` event and the incident or maintenance record used to disposition it. These artifacts show what the kernel attributes reported to Splunk; they do not prove collection completeness, successful repair, or data integrity.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index, ingest one in-window event with `host=raid-test-positive`, `collector_status=ok`, `md_device=md0`, `raid_level=raid5`, `raid_disks=3`, `degraded=1`, `array_state=active`, `sync_action=recover`, `sync_completed=4096/8192`, and `faulty_components=sdb1`. Run a copy of the SPL against that index with fixed time bounds. Expect exactly one row for `md0` with `degraded_devices=1` and `rebuild_percent=50.0`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In the same test index, ingest a newer event for `host=raid-test-negative`, `md_device=md1`, with `collector_status=ok`, `raid_level=raid1`, `raid_disks=2`, `degraded=0`, `array_state=clean`, `sync_action=idle`, `sync_completed=none`, and `faulty_components=none`. Expect zero rows. Separately set `degraded=unknown` or `collector_status=unreadable` and confirm malformed or failed collection is excluded from the degradation result and appears in the collection-health search instead.

dataSources: A custom read-only scripted input runs on each Linux Splunk Universal Forwarder every 60 seconds and reads the kernel's documented md sysfs attributes under `/sys/block/md*/md`. It sends one key-value event per active md array to the deployment-selected `index=os` with the locally defined `sourcetype=linux:md_raid`. Required event fields are `collector_status`, `md_device`, `raid_level`, `raid_disks`, `degraded`, `array_state`, `sync_action`, `sync_completed`, and `faulty_components`; Splunk supplies `_time` and `host`. Neither the sourcetype nor these normalized field names is supplied by Splunk or `Splunk_TA_nix`.
app: A local deployment app containing the supplied scripted input for the Splunk Universal Forwarder plus matching parsing and search-time sourcetype settings; no Splunkbase or premium app is required.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=linux:md_raid earliest=-10m@m latest=@m
| fields _time host collector_status md_device raid_level raid_disks degraded array_state sync_action sync_completed faulty_components
| eval raid_disks=tonumber(raid_disks), degraded_devices=tonumber(degraded)
| where collector_status="ok" AND isnotnull(host) AND isnotnull(md_device) AND isnotnull(raid_level) AND raid_disks>0 AND degraded_devices>=0
| sort 0 - _time
| dedup host md_device
| where degraded_devices>0
| rex field=sync_completed "^(?<sync_completed_sectors>\d+)/(?<sync_total_sectors>\d+)$"
| eval sync_completed_sectors=tonumber(sync_completed_sectors), sync_total_sectors=tonumber(sync_total_sectors), rebuild_percent=if(sync_total_sectors>0,round(100*sync_completed_sectors/sync_total_sectors,1),null()), observed_at=_time
| table observed_at host md_device raid_level raid_disks degraded_devices array_state sync_action sync_completed rebuild_percent faulty_components
| sort 0 -degraded_devices host md_device
description: Reports the latest valid sample for each Linux host and active md array in the preceding 10 minutes when the kernel exposes one or more missing devices in the array's `degraded` sysfs attribute. Each row identifies the array and RAID level, gives the exact missing-device count and current array state, and adds recovery progress when `sync_completed` contains a numeric sector fraction.
value: A redundant array can continue serving I/O after a member is lost, leaving operators unaware that fault tolerance has narrowed or disappeared. Promptly exposing the kernel's missing-device count helps the storage owner confirm the fault, protect the workload, and begin an approved replacement or recovery procedure before another failure causes an outage or data loss.
implementation: Deploy the supplied sysfs collector through a local Universal Forwarder app, emit one event per active md array every 60 seconds, and verify the normalized fields against the same host's sysfs files and `mdadm --detail --test`. Schedule the latest-state search every five minutes over a complete 10-minute window and alert on any `degraded_devices>0`; zero versus greater than zero is a kernel-defined count boundary, not a tunable performance threshold.
visualization: Use a latest-state alert table keyed by `host` and `md_device`, showing missing-device count, level, array state, recovery action and progress, and known faulty components. Add a recovery-progress line or single-value panel only while `sync_action` is active, plus a separate expected-host/array freshness panel so absent collection cannot look healthy.

knownFalsePositives:
The rule reports a real nonzero kernel degradation count, but paging can still be non-actionable in these bounded cases:

1. **Approved member-replacement exercise** — An operator may intentionally fail and remove one component before adding its replacement. Confirm the exact `host`, `md_device`, failed member, change ticket, and maintenance interval with `mdadm --detail`; mute notification routing only for that array and interval while retaining result rows.

2. **Expected recovery already in progress** — `sync_action=recover` and an advancing numeric `sync_completed` fraction can mean a spare is rebuilding successfully, but the array remains degraded until recovery completes. Attach updates to the existing incident instead of opening duplicates; do not suppress the underlying state or assume progress guarantees completion.

3. **Non-atomic read during a rapid state transition** — The collector reads separate sysfs files sequentially, so a member failure or completed recovery can briefly pair a new `degraded` count with an adjacent old state value. Compare the next poll and read the same attributes or run `mdadm --detail --test` on the host. A persistent nonzero count is not a parsing false positive.

4. **Delayed or replayed event after maintenance** — Forwarder backlog can deliver a formerly degraded sample after the array is healthy. Compare `observed_at`, `_indextime`, the latest raw event, and live kernel state; repair forwarding delay rather than creating an open-ended exception.

**Safe suppression:** keep the primary SPL unchanged. If routing policy requires maintenance exceptions, apply a separate owner-approved lookup after the base result, keyed by exact `host` and `md_device`, with start epoch, end epoch, ticket, reason, and approver. Preserve suppressed matches for review and reject wildcards or non-expiring entries.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and measurement boundary

Assign a Linux storage owner and a Splunk content owner. Use this implementation only for active Linux md arrays represented by `/sys/block/md*/md`. The kernel documents `degraded` as the count of devices by which a redundant array is degraded: zero is optimal and one means one failed or missing device. It separately documents `array_state`, `raid_disks`, `sync_action`, and `sync_completed`. This search therefore uses `degraded>0` as its only fault threshold. It does not infer health from a free-text status label, an underscore in `/proc/mdstat`, or an undocumented `status` field.

Deploy a supported Splunk Universal Forwarder or another approved scripted-input execution tier on each in-scope Linux host. The service account needs read and traverse access to `/sys/block/md*/md`; it needs no permission to write sysfs, fail a component, stop an array, or run privileged repair commands. Test access under the actual service identity. The Splunk role needs read access to the chosen operating-system index and permission to schedule an alert. This record uses `index=os` as a deployment choice; change both the input stanza and SPL if the approved index has another name.

Inventory expected hosts and arrays outside the detection. A stopped, disappeared, or never-assembled array may not have `/sys/block/mdX/md`, so polling only present directories cannot prove that every expected array exists. RAID0 and linear arrays have no redundant-member failure semantics; the upstream mdadm manual says monitor mode is meaningful for RAID1, 4, 5, 6, 10, and multipath arrays. Route unsupported levels and missing expected arrays to collection or configuration health rather than treating absence as zero degradation. Keep `mdmonitor.service` or the site's supported mdadm monitor configuration as an independent local notification path; this Splunk search should not be the host's sole warning mechanism.

## 1. Collect normalized kernel attributes

Package `collect_md_raid.sh` from `scriptExample` as `$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/linux_md_raid/bin/collect_md_raid.sh`, owned by the forwarder account and executable. The app and `linux:md_raid` sourcetype are local conventions, not Splunkbase products and not content supplied by `Splunk_TA_nix`. Configure the app's `local/inputs.conf`:

```ini
[script://./bin/collect_md_raid.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
index = os
sourcetype = linux:md_raid
```

Splunk documents that scripted inputs can run on a Universal Forwarder, that the interval is measured in seconds, and that scripts belong in an app's `bin` directory. On the parsing tier, configure `[linux:md_raid]` with `SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false` and `DATETIME_CONFIG=CURRENT`; every output line is one event and has no embedded timestamp. On the search tier, retain key-value extraction for the emitted `name=value` pairs. Distribute parsing and search knowledge to the appropriate tiers instead of assuming the forwarder app alone makes fields available everywhere.

The script emits one line per active md array. It removes whitespace from scalar sysfs values, reports missing required attributes as `collector_status=unreadable`, and turns a numeric `sync_completed` fraction into the whitespace-free form `completed/total`. `sync_action=not_applicable` and `sync_completed=none` are context values when those files are absent or contain no fraction; neither is a degradation signal. `faulty_components` is a comma-delimited hint derived from component `state` files containing `faulty` or `blocked`; the authoritative trigger remains the numeric array-level `degraded` value. Because separate files are read sequentially, one event is not an atomic kernel snapshot.

At a 60-second interval, the expected volume is 1,440 events per active array per day. Verify that the script exits promptly and emits only stdout events; Splunk sends script stderr to `splunkd.log`. If the collector emits `collector_status=no_arrays`, retain it for inventory diagnostics but do not interpret it as healthy RAID. Validate field extraction with `index=os sourcetype=linux:md_raid earliest=-10m` and confirm that numeric fields are not embedded in `_raw` only.

## 2. Save and understand the detection

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_md_raid_degraded_array_10m`. Schedule it every five minutes after the indexing boundary, for example at minute 2, 7, 12, and so on, while the explicit `earliest=-10m@m latest=@m` covers complete minute buckets. Alert when result count is greater than zero. The two-sample-width window tolerates a delayed poll; it is not a requirement that degradation persist for 10 minutes.

The search converts `raid_disks` and `degraded` with `tonumber` and rejects failed collection, missing identity, nonpositive configured member counts, and nonnumeric or negative degradation values. It sorts newest first and `dedup`s by `host` and `md_device`, so an older degraded sample does not fire after a newer healthy sample in the same window. The final `where degraded_devices>0` is an exact device count in units of missing members. It is not a percentage and has no vendor-published warning band to tune. Any nonzero count warrants investigation because the remaining tolerance depends on RAID level, layout, concurrent errors, and workload; do not label `degraded=1` universally safe or `degraded=2` universally failed.

The `rex` expression accepts only `digits/digits` from `sync_completed`. When the total is positive, `rebuild_percent` is the completed-sector fraction multiplied by 100 and rounded to one decimal place. It is progress for the current kernel sync action, not an estimated completion time, throughput value, proof that recovery is healthy, or an alert threshold. `array_state` values such as `active`, `clean`, `readonly`, `read-auto`, `inactive`, and `write-pending` are context. Do not replace the degradation rule with a guessed list of good or bad state words.

Route the first result for an array to the Linux storage owner at the service's approved urgency. Deduplicate subsequent notifications by exact host and md device in the incident system while preserving each scheduled result. A recovery that remains degraded belongs to the same incident, but a higher missing-device count or a stopped recovery should update urgency immediately. Do not use a long Splunk throttle that can hide those changes.

## 3. Validate collection and SPL logic

On a staging host with an already configured md array, compare one indexed event with direct reads of `/sys/block/<md_device>/md/level`, `raid_disks`, `degraded`, `array_state`, `sync_action`, and `sync_completed` within one collection interval. Then run `mdadm --detail --test /dev/<md_device>` under the site's approved privilege model. Upstream mdadm documents exit 0 for normal operation, 1 for at least one failed device, 2 when multiple failures make the array unusable, and 4 for an information error. Use that command as an independent validation point; do not map its exit code numerically onto the kernel's degradation count.

Exercise the `controlTest` with synthetic key-value events in an isolated test index and fixed time bounds. The positive row must return `degraded_devices=1` and 50.0 percent progress. The healthy row must return no result. Add two samples for the same host and array—an older `degraded=1` followed by a newer `degraded=0`—and verify `dedup` keeps the healthy sample. Reverse the values and verify one result. Test exact boundaries: zero must not fire and one must fire. Confirm `degraded=unknown`, a missing `raid_disks`, and `collector_status=unreadable` do not become zero or an alert.

Do not fail a production disk merely to test this content. If a lab owner conducts a controlled mdadm failure and recovery exercise, follow upstream and operating-system procedures, use disposable data, and obtain explicit change approval. This editorial review specifies synthetic logic and host comparison only; it did not execute the collector on an md host, index fixtures, run SPL in Splunk, alter an array, or validate an alert action.

Build a separate freshness search from an authoritative expected-host/array inventory. At a 60-second poll, a continuously connected array should normally produce several events in five minutes, allowing for script runtime and forwarding delay. Alert on missing expected identities and on `collector_status` values other than `ok`. This closes the central blind spot: no degradation row can mean healthy, missing collection, lost forwarder connectivity, or an array that disappeared.

## 4. Dashboard, response, and evidence

Use a latest-state table with `host`, `md_device`, `raid_level`, `raid_disks`, `degraded_devices`, `array_state`, `sync_action`, `rebuild_percent`, `faulty_components`, and `observed_at`. Add a drilldown to the raw events and a progress panel only where a numeric total exists. Put collection freshness beside the fault table and visibly distinguish `no_arrays`, `unreadable`, and missing expected data from a healthy zero count.

When an alert fires, first verify the latest kernel attributes and `mdadm --detail --test` on the same host. Confirm the array identity, level, missing count, component state, current sync action, and whether progress advances between polls. Review kernel and mdadm logs near the first nonzero sample, then follow the platform's md RAID runbook. Protect application writes and backups according to service policy before replacement work. Never automate `mdadm --fail`, `--remove`, `--add`, `--assemble --force`, filesystem changes, or reboot actions from this detection; those commands can affect availability and data safety and require storage-owner judgment.

After recovery, require a later event with `degraded=0`, confirm the expected component membership and normal mdadm test result, and watch for recurrent component errors. Retain the first alert, state changes, raw samples, incident timeline, operator validation, and approved remediation record under local retention policy. The saved-search artifacts establish observed telemetry and response, not that data was uncorrupted or restored from backup.

## 5. Troubleshoot and suppress safely

No events from one host: verify app deployment, executable mode, scripted-input status, index routing, forwarder connectivity, and read access under the forwarder account. Use `splunk btool inputs list --debug` and inspect `splunkd.log` for script stderr or timeout. `collector_status=unreadable`: identify the exact missing sysfs attribute on the host; do not fabricate a default zero. Fields visible only in `_raw`: restore the parsing/search-tier settings for this local sourcetype. Duplicate events: look for duplicate input stanzas or two forwarders collecting the same host.

A `degraded` count that disagrees with nearby state context can arise during a state transition because the files are read independently. Compare the next poll and live sysfs before diagnosing extraction drift. A stale degraded result after repair requires checking `_indextime`, queues, and latest ordering. An array absent from the dashboard must be compared with inventory and `/proc/mdstat`; absence is not proof of health.

Keep maintenance suppression outside the primary detection so the observable rule remains reviewable. Match exact `host` and `md_device`, require bounded start and end epochs plus owner, ticket, reason, and approver, and preserve suppressed rows. Do not suppress all arrays on a host, all recovery actions, or all events with an expected faulty component: a second member can fail during the same maintenance window.
grandmaExplanation: We watch Linux servers for a group of disks that has lost one or more members. The group may still be working, but the warning gives the storage team time to confirm the problem and repair it before another failure causes a bigger outage.
scriptExample:
#!/bin/sh
# Read-only collector for active Linux md array attributes.
found=0

for md_path in /sys/block/md*/md; do
  [ -d "$md_path" ] || continue
  found=1
  md_device=${md_path%/md}
  md_device=${md_device##*/}
  collector_status=ok

  raid_level=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$md_path/level" 2>/dev/null) || collector_status=unreadable
  raid_disks=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$md_path/raid_disks" 2>/dev/null) || collector_status=unreadable
  degraded=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$md_path/degraded" 2>/dev/null) || collector_status=unreadable
  array_state=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$md_path/array_state" 2>/dev/null) || collector_status=unreadable

  [ -n "$raid_level" ] || raid_level=unknown
  [ -n "$raid_disks" ] || raid_disks=unknown
  [ -n "$degraded" ] || degraded=unknown
  [ -n "$array_state" ] || array_state=unknown

  sync_action=not_applicable
  if [ -r "$md_path/sync_action" ]; then
    sync_action=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$md_path/sync_action" 2>/dev/null) || collector_status=unreadable
    [ -n "$sync_action" ] || sync_action=unknown
  fi

  sync_completed=none
  if [ -r "$md_path/sync_completed" ]; then
    sync_completed=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$md_path/sync_completed" 2>/dev/null) || collector_status=unreadable
    [ -n "$sync_completed" ] || sync_completed=none
  fi

  faulty_components=
  for state_file in "$md_path"/dev-*/state; do
    [ -r "$state_file" ] || continue
    component=${state_file%/state}
    component=${component##*/dev-}
    component_state=$(tr -d '[:space:]' < "$state_file" 2>/dev/null) || collector_status=unreadable
    case ",$component_state," in
      *,faulty,*|*,blocked,*)
        if [ -n "$faulty_components" ]; then
          faulty_components=$faulty_components,$component
        else
          faulty_components=$component
        fi
        ;;
    esac
  done
  [ -n "$faulty_components" ] || faulty_components=none

  case "$raid_disks:$degraded" in
    *[!0-9:]*|:*|*:)
      collector_status=unreadable
      ;;
  esac

  printf 'collector_status=%s md_device=%s raid_level=%s raid_disks=%s degraded=%s array_state=%s sync_action=%s sync_completed=%s faulty_components=%s\n' \
    "$collector_status" "$md_device" "$raid_level" "$raid_disks" "$degraded" "$array_state" "$sync_action" "$sync_completed" "$faulty_components"
done

if [ "$found" -eq 0 ]; then
  printf '%s\n' 'collector_status=no_arrays md_device=none raid_level=unknown raid_disks=unknown degraded=unknown array_state=unknown sync_action=not_applicable sync_completed=none faulty_components=none'
fi
